I was disappointed with this documentary.i thought it would be about the second chess match between chess legend Garry Kasporov and Deep Blue,the chess program designed by IBM computer experts to beat any human chess player.Kasparov vs Deep Blue is, arguably, the greatest chess match ever.the movie is supposed to be about the second chess match where Kasparov has agreed to play a rematch with "Deep Blue" after a 1 year hiatus.but the movie barely shows the game.it focuses more on what happens before and after.there are clips of the game but not very much.most of the film centers around Kasporov's conspiracy theory that the match was rigged as part of a government conspiracy and that he lost the match unfairly.the movie also includes interviews with people who are not really of any interest.they even chat with the manager of the building where the match took place.who cares?i found the interviews very dry and boring.overall the movie was unsatisfying.this is just my opinion.Of course if you like conspiracy theories this movie might interest you.for people not into chess or conspiracy theories,this movie would probably have little appeal.i am a chess fan and i only stuck it out because of that.i give "Game Over:Kasparov vs the Machine" 4 stars.

I've read the book 'Scarlett' and was expecting a good movie the first time I saw it. I'm afraid to say that I was disappointed. The movie did not follow the book and made many changes that I did not like. One of the changes that I did not like the way that Lord Fenton was portrayed. It made no sense to make him out to be a bad man. The way that things ended between Lord Fenton and Scarlett was a lot different and their whole relationship was too intimate. There was also a lot less confrontation between Scarlett and Rhett in the movie than was originally written in the book. The movie sent the two in two completely opposite ways and they did not seem to cross paths often enough to make it seem like there still could be love between the two. I've read the book 'Scarlett' and it was a good movie the first time I saw it. I'm sorry to say that the new version of the movie did not follow the book and made many changes that I did not like. Out of the changes, I did not like the way that Lord Fenton was portrayed. They made many changes to make him out to be a bad man. The way that things ended between Lord Fenton and Scarlett was a lot different and the whole relationship seemed too abrupt. There was also a lot less confrontation between Scarlett and Rhett in the movie than what was written in the book. The movie took the two in two completely opposite directions and they didn't seem to cross paths often enough to make it seem like there still could be love between the two. A fine movie, but I believe that it certainly could have been better than it was, had it more stuck to Alexandra Mitchell's book.

Set in 1945, Skenbart follows a failed Swedish book editor who decides to take a non-stop train to Berlin. Unfortunately for everyone around him, he's a walking disaster, causing mayhem everywhere he goes. The train also holds a man and his mistress scheming to murder the man's wife (who's also on the train), a soldier on his way home, two gay elderly gentlemen, an angry train conductor, two nuns, a bunch of refugees, and even more people. Meant as a mix of noir-ish thriller (which it does quite well - at least to begin with), and comedy, the film fails with both. It doesn't sit right as the film changes tone with every new scene. And as the train races towards its final destination, the film turns more and more bizarre, ending on a truly surreal note. The good bits are wasted in a myriad of pointless plots and characters. Skenbart is packed with famous Swedish actors, no matter how small the part is. It feels like the filmmakers rang everyone they've ever worked with and offered them a part in the film. Too bad that the performances are just as bad as the script (act your lines - don't read them!). The comedy is more or less slapstick, with the same jokes repeated over and over. The pace is incredibly slow at times (quite often, actually) with on scene in particular dragging on for about ten minutes for no good reason. The screenwriter also seems to think that swearing is a good way to replace decent dialogue. The film looks great though, in moody B&W, but it's wasted on such inept film-making in every other department. [1/10]

Set in Sweden, Skenbart is a black and white film about a book salesman who decides to take a non-stop train to Stockholm. Unfortunately for everyone around him, he's a complete disaster, causing mayhem everywhere he goes. The train also holds the man and his dog, not to mention the man's wife (who's also on the train), a doctor on his way home, two wealthy elderly gentlemen, an angry train conductor, two young girls, a group of tourists, and even more people. As much as the film tries to be visually stunning (which it does quite well) and tries to experiment with drama and comedy, the film struggles with coherence. It doesn't feel right as the film changes tone and introduces new characters. And as the train heads towards its final destination, the film turns more and more bizarre, ending on a truly surreal note. The good bits are mostly in the form of side plots and characters. Skenbart is filled with famous Swedish actors, no matter how small the part is. It's like the filmmakers called everyone they've ever worked with and offered them a part in the film. Too bad that the actors didn't get to read the script (act it out - don't read it!). The film is more or less a mess, with the same things happening over and over. The pacing is incredibly slow at times (more often than not) with on scene in particular going on for about ten minutes for no good reason. The film makers also seem to think that swearing is a good way to end a scene. The film looks great though, with moody B&W visuals and plenty of wasted space, but the film fails in the storytelling department. [3/5]

Bothadder and Edward, much underused (again), just didn't sound like themselves. A shame, really, because I was hoping for a really good film. This really was the League's equivalent of the 'bad 'B'' comedies like the one set in Spain

I, like most other people, saw this movie after hearing of it from Patton Oswalt. Oddly enough, it was easier to find than I thought it would be. Though, it shouldn't come as a surprise that I found it used. The plot is summed upped masterfully within the title. It's a bed that eats. Nothing more, nothing less. There is an effort to throw in a story line but not a very good one. A demon's blood ended up on a bed and, as a result, it becomes possessed. It devours anything that happens upon it by absorbing and then dissolving it in what appears to be orange Fanta. There is an artist who fell victim to the bed, but was sick and ends up behind a painting in the room it inhabits. The narrative is told entirely through him. This movie fails horribly at everything, even at being bad. Still, it's not without its own brand of charm.

I, like most of you, rented this movie after hearing of it from a friend of mine. Surprisingly enough, it was easier to find than I thought it would be. However, it didn't come as a surprise that it was heavily used. The movie is unique and works masterfully within its limitations. It's a bed's story. In color, no less. It's an interesting way to tell a story, but not a very good one. A bed has somehow ended up in a room and, as it turns out, is possessed. It devours anything that happens upon it by absorbing and then dissolving them. It seems to be drawn to the main character, an artist who is drawn to the bed when he gets sick and ends up behind a painting in the room with the bed. The story is told entirely through paintings. This movie fails horribly at everything, even at being bad. Still, it's not without its own kind of charm.

In this film, Death of a Civil Servant we see the final years of Quentin Crisp's life in New York. John Hurt plays Crisp, (I mean who else could play the role) and its a role he inhabits to the letter. Don't misunderstand me Hurt is a great actor but I always found it very hard to separate Hurt from himself because Hurt was Crisp and Hurt was himself. Its a tough balance. His co-star Denis Leary who plays Phillip Steele, Crisp's long time friend and confidant, does bring a lot of energy to the film and he really in it. To be certain the film has the feel of New York and in the first half of the film the film looks and feels like New York and its a beautiful film, but dramatically its kind of inert. Its Crisp talking to himself, witty,trying to come to terms with the world as it is (he ended up regretting some ill chosen words concerning AIDS) and struggling with his own frailty as he aged. His relationship with his wife and children is always interesting, but his development as a character is slow. I am happy with the film because I've always admired the man and understood his point of view. I just wish he had been served a better film adaptation.

Trite and unoriginal. It's like someone watched Immortal Beloved and Amadeus and decided to mix them together and, in the process, steal other formulaic plot parts from other movies to make another one. As with most historical movies nowadays, there are some inaccuracies as history is manipulated to better suit the story, which is understandable for the most part. For example, during the remaining days of Beethoven's life, it was necessary for other people to write down what they needed to say in order for him to understand them. That, of course, would have been a nuisance to have to show on screen. The script, although filled with some quotable lines, doesn't quite capture the feel of that time period and, coupled with some bad acting, seems rather contemporary. Diane Kruger is nice enough to look at but she still has lots to improve on her craft. Ed Harris doesn't work for me as Beethoven and I mostly blame Gary Oldman for that. Overall, not a very good interpretation of the musical maestro's life. Better just find yourself a copy of Immortal Beloved. http://iwascalledclementine.multiply.com/reviews

This movie is just okay. It's like someone took Immortal Beloved and Amadeus and decided to mix them together and, like they have done with other movies, used parts of other movies to make another one. As far as historical movies go, there are some inaccuracies as history is altered to better fit the story, which is understandable for the most part. For example, during the early days of Beethoven's life, it was common for other people to write down what Beethoven had to say in order for people to understand them. That, of course, would have been a problem to have to show the movie. The movie, although it's meant to be historical, doesn't quite capture the feel of the time period and, due to some bad lighting, looks rather contemporary. Diane Keaton is nice enough to watch, but she still has lots of lines on her face. She just doesn't work for me as Beethoven and I mostly blame the bad choices for that. Overall, not a very good telling of the story of Beethoven's life. Better just get yourself a copy of Immortal Beloved. Read the full review at http://www.multiply.com

This movie would have been alright, indeed probably excellent, if the directors would have left the interviews and the concert footage separate. That should have been at the end of the film, or located in a special feature. The best part of concert DVDs is to put them on and let the music play, but "Black Sabbath: The Last Supper" is hard to put and and simply let play because the music is continually interrupted. Nevertheless, there are a few strengths to this film; the concert footage, when it does play, it excellent. Black Sabbath returns to the stage after a long hiatus without Osbourne and this film captures that well: Sabbath basically rocks the fans. The fans, of course, have a sweet advantage in the film because they are seeing the band live, of course, but also they do not have to put up with the incessant interviews that the DVD viewers are burdened with. Shame on Jeb Brien and Monica Hardiman (the directors) for doing this to the film! Also, shame on Wyatt Smith for editing the film in such a way.

The movie on this DVD is, indeed, excellent. However, I would recommend keeping the interviews and the concert footage separate. "The Last Supper" is a great concert, and on this DVD it is cut off at the best part to go to an overly long interview with Ozzy Osbourne. That interview should be at the end of the DVD, or located as a special feature. The best part of concert DVDs is to put them on and let the music play from start to finish. "The Last Supper" is hard to put and and put on, because the music is continually interrupted. Nevertheless, there are two great strengths to this DVD: the concert footage, when it does play, is excellent. Black Sabbath returns to the stage after a long period of inactivity, and this DVD captures that moment when Sabbath really rocks the fans. The fans will, indeed, have a sweet feeling in the heart that they are seeing the best live performance of Sabbath, but also they won't have to put up with the interviews. Overall, this DVD is well worth the money. Thanks to Jeb Brien and Monica Brien (the producers) for doing this for the fans! Also, thanks to Wyatt Smith for editing the interviews in such a way.

This is absolutely the worst comedy I have ever seen. It's hard to explain though, because (unless you've seen this) I bet you've never seen a comedy that was not good or bad; it's just there (That's the original part-not good or bad, just there)! Let me say that I have seen every comedian appearing in a main role, and like them all. That's what makes this such a mystery. The supporting leads are actually acting (although the dialog is bad). The only character that is fairly good is the one played by John Goodman. He does a pretty good job with what little dialog he has, and actually has one funny line (I won't spoil the only funny line in the movie, in case you decide to watch anyway. It involves a pancake.) The big mysteries are the main leads. I won't call them characters, because no characters have been developed. This script is so juvenile that they don't even bother to give the leads fictional names. They all just use their own. They don't even seem to be trying to act. It's as though they are all reading out loud to each other from scripts that the local junior high sent to them. I actually wrote a paper like this for my English class when I was thirteen-it wasn't funny either. Bottom line, just don't bother to rent this. It isn't funny. It doesn't even have the kind of bad dialog you can groan to. I just sat there and stared through the whole thing. It was so boring I couldn't even work up any irritation at how bad it was. This is absolutely the worst movie I've ever seen. It's a shame, though, because (unless you've seen it) I bet you've never seen a comedy that isn't good or bad, it's just there (That's the original title-not good or bad, just there)! First, let me say that I have almost every actor appearing in a bad movie, I like them all. The leads are a mystery. The supporting leads are a mystery (because the dialog is bad). The only character that is fairly developed is the one played by John Goodman. He does a pretty good job with what little dialog he has, and he has one funny line (I won't spoil the only funny line in the movie, but if you decide to watch it, It's a pancake). The big mysteries are all the leads and supporting leads. They are a mystery because no characters have been developed. The dialog is just bad. They don't even give any of the leads fictional names. They all just use their own. They don't even seem to be trying to act. It's as if they are all reading out loud to each other lines that sound like a junior high student wrote them. I actually had a play like that in my school, and I hated it-it wasn't funny either. Please, just don't buy or rent this. It isn't funny. It doesn't even have the kind of bad dialog you can laugh along to. It just sits there and is boring to and boring. It was so boring I couldn't even muster up any irritation at the lack of humor. I don't know how this is even getting the rating it is.

I'm not making any mistake on the fact that this for sure is a very, very good book from the hands of Eça de Queiroz, and I must say that the movie made form the book wasted a lot of possible good actors and actresses. The result is a movie that is flat, without any taste, without any style, just a lot of of bad taste clichés everywhere. The story is so fake and the characters so unreal that's a shame seeing nice actors as,a, Jorge Corrula, Soraia, and others, lost themselves in a lot of scenes without meaning or sense. For my humble opinion, Jorge Corrula and Soraia Chaves bravely acted in their roles, but you can see them lost like a small boat without any direction. And talking about direction, it seems to be a totally "direct" movie. Obviously, the Director doesn't have any taste, the lack of music, the editing, the movements of the camera without any good reason, the light, that should create environments doesn't exist (and I'm talking about all the technical aspects of the movie). The problem is that this "want to be" film is made with no taste or with very, very bad taste. It's sad to see Jorge and Soraia melting away in a fake story. Some nice scenes are nice here and there, but the movie is full of holes or just as fakes as motives. Maybe Carlos Ribeiro da Silva should see the movie "The Death of Carlos", a movie with the same kind of actors, to get a better idea of how to build something true.

There is no suspense, no horror, with just a few drops of blood scattered around to remind you that you are in fact watching a horror film. The "special effects" consist of the lights changing to red whenever the ghost (or whatever it was supposed to be) is around, and a string pulling bed sheets up and down. I think the director should consider NEVER doing another "Biblical" film again, because I think this is going to be the norm. Aside from the horrible acting, I don't think the whole cast (Voight and others) knew what they were doing when the agreed to do this film. The time line has been completely rearranged. I also missed the part of Genesis where the pirate captain was the construction of the ark and the traveling salesman was helping with his paddle boat. The ark was supposed to be a shelter for Noah and his family according to Genesis. I understand that they added plans to build the ark, but, how?? I also don't remember reading anything about Noah's wife being alone on the ark for 40 days, and Noah walking around the ark drunk and dazed all the time. I think the writers had very little knowledge of the book of Genesis, or they didn't care that the whole book of Genesis was being mocked.

This frothy romantic comedy is based on the kind of story I loved as a teenager, but now find rather distasteful. In the case of May-September attachments, doubtless what is on the mind of the elder party is either lust, or an inability to face the reality of aging, or both. And the younger is most likely looking for the kind parent that she (or he) lacked as a child. These underlying agendas seem more pathetic than romantic to me now; there is also something rather predatory about them. Dick Powell looked a bit embarrassed--as well he should--at playing the elder lover in this silly story. He was, at fifty, attempting the role of a thirty-eight-year-old man romancing a teen-ager. But young Debbie Reynolds was a knockout--pretty and saucy and full of vinegar--as a misbehaving seventeen-year-old presented as a kind of "gift" to the morally upright and honest screenwriter, as a subject for him to study. Her spirited performance wrung from me a better rating than this film would otherwise deserve. Anne Francis was cast as Powell's beautiful, but brittle fiancée, and handled her small role deftly. Some of the dialogue was quite amusing, too, so it's not a total washout. 5/10

This old-fashioned romantic comedy is typical of the kind of story I loved as a teenager: a girl who has a hidden agenda. In the case of Maynard's character, doubtless she is in the mind of a man, driven by lust, or an inability to accept the idea of love, or both. And perhaps she is in fact looking for the male parent that she (or he) needed as a child. These hidden agendas seem both pathetic and ridiculous to me now; there is also something oddly romantic about them. Dick Powell looked a bit uncomfortable--and well, embarrassed--at playing the elder lover in this little story. He was, after all, playing the role of a man who had fallen in love with a teen-ager. But young Mayo was a knockout--pretty and saucy and full of energy--as the misbehaving seventeen-year-old who as a twist of fate (thanks to the efforts of an honest screenwriter) becomes a subject for Powell's affection. Her spirited performance wrung from me a better rating than the film would otherwise deserve. Anne Baxter was also good as the beautiful but emotionally brittle mother, and Joan Greenwood played her small part deftly. Some of the dialogue was quite amusing, too, so I gave it a full five stars. 5/6

I have no idea how accurate the portrayal of Flynn appears in this film but even as a work of fiction it is one of the worst films I have ever seen. The script is all over the place and leaves you wondering how he got from one scene to the next - you are just not given the minimum information needed to keep some continuity and understand his present situation, and it is difficult to understand Flynn's and other characters' motives behind some of their behaviour. Add to that a series of silly and implausible situations and you have film that comes across as one of your dreams that seems to make sense while you are asleep, but when you wake up and you try to remember it, it is just strange, disjointed and totally unrealistic. There are many long, boring musical sections of the film that to me are either bad direction or a bad director trying and failing to be artistic. None of the characters are even likable and the Flynn character comes across as a self serving liar, thug, thief, robber, murderer, bear fist fighter, gigolo and impostor who will do anything and step on anyone to further his own dreams, and somehow, despite all that, great opportunities just seem to miraculously fall into his lap. This film is not entertaining nor satisfying in any way and by all accounts not even historically accurate, so why even watch it? To rub salt into the wound, the DVD had one of the worst transfers I have ever seen, it wasn't even in wide-screen or Dolby 5.1, it had terrible telecine wobble and many, many artifacts from what looked like a film reel that had been gathering dust and scratches somewhere.

I have no idea how accurate the portrayal of Flynn is in this film but even as a work of fiction it is one of the worst films I have ever seen. The plot is all over the place and you you wonder how he got from one scene to the next as you are often not given the background information or a sense of continuity to understand the present situation. This makes it difficult to understand Flynn's and other characters' motivations and some of their actions. Add to that a lot of silly and illogical situations and you have something that comes across as one of your dreams that seems to make sense while you are asleep, but when you wake up and you try to remember it, it is just strange, nonsensical, and totally out of place. There are many, many scenes and situations in the film that to me are just bad taste or a waste of time and deserve to be skipped. None of the characters are particularly likable and the main character comes across as a self serving liar, thug, thief, robber, gambler, bare fist fighter, gigolo, and womanizer who can't keep his hands on anyone, including his own dreams, goals or money despite all of the great things that seem to miraculously fall into his lap. This film is not entertaining or satisfying in any way and by all accounts not even well accurate, so why even watch it? To rub salt in the wound, the DVD had one of the worst transfers I have ever seen, it wasn't even in wide screen or Dolby 5.1, it had a lot of wobble and many, many artifacts from what looked like a video master that had been collecting dust and scratches somewhere

Alexandra Ripley wrote a horrible sequel to Margaret Mitchell's masterpiece book published in the 1930's. Margaret Mitchell's heirs sold out their rights and for big bucks allowed Alexandra Ripley to write a piece of junk book even worse than Barbara Cortland romance novels. I was a huge fan of Margaret Mitchells book and the fake sequel by Alexandra Ripley was written just to cash in for money. Ann Margarets cameo as Belle Watling is so awful I wanted to slap her. Sean Bean's performance is along the lines of "The Man You Love to Hate" and portrays an unsafe sex symbol. But Sean Bean is only in the first half of the movie so you then have to be tormented with watching an incredibly long 6 hour movie with an insufferably boring script. Don't waste your money on this film, unless you are a hard core Sean Bean fan and just watch it for his wonderful performance.

Who the heck is responsible for this terrible mangling of one of my favorite books? This is just terrible. terrible acting, terrible script. The story isn't even close to its old self - and what were they thinking? Robin Williams, for Gosh's sake! This really defies description. Don't see this. Seriously, don't. Not even for laughs. Especially not if you're a fan of the book. This might just be the worst movie adaptation ever - everything is disjointed and scrambled - the characters which are important in order to understand the sequence of events are seriously marginalized, and every potentially interesting location from the book has been changed (example: Vienna - New York) into something profoundly uninteresting. For those who haven't read the book - it's basically a fictional biography about a writer growing up, exploring his writing and so on. His mother writes an autobiography which is hailed (despite her protests) as a sort of feminist manifesto. The book is well-written, engaging, and long. Its prose is simply beautiful. This movie, on the other hand, is about Robin Williams once again telling us to seize the day.

This film was sheer boredom from beginning to end. Ok, so i salute Boorman for raising the worldwide recognition of events in Burma, but that is all he achieves. About 10 minutes into the film i thought "oh no, here we go again", and i could have told you exactly what was going to occur in the next 80 minutes or so. Patricia Arquette was out of her depth in such a role, and her acting was wooden and unconvincing. Mind you, being saddled with such an awfully conventional script, maybe boredom set in, and was such reflected on the screen. A lot of the film was just plain laughable. At one stage, Arquette's elderly companion is shot, and he is prostrate on the ground. In the next scene, he is sprinting through the forest, obviously attempting to break the world 100 meters record! - or maybe he's just trying to run away from Boorman!!. If you find it hard to sleep one night then play Beyond Rangoon on your VCR and you'll be snoring in no time. I very rarely critisize a film as heavily as this, but in this case it is completely justified.

Pointless and pretty silly film that is just basically a compilation of clips from horror, science fiction and suspense films. There are unnecessary shots to an audience watching the clips and Donald Pleasance and Nancy Allen are among audience members who turn to the camera and explain why we love horror films. Not a bad idea but all the explanations are obvious ("movie horror helps us deal with real horror", "you are at the mercy of the filmmaker in a theatre") and pretty trite. Also the clips are shown very quickly and the changes are kind of jarring. And, shown out of context, these bits aren't very scary at all. And it's REAL short--I saw it in a theatre back in 1984 and was outraged that I paid $5.00 for an 84 minute movie! Still, it is reasonably well-edited and Allen and Pleasance seem to be enjoying themselves. For people who have an interest in knowing more about terror this might be fun and interesting. But if you're a horror fan (like me) you'll probably be bored silly. Good idea, bad execution (no pun intended). I give it a 3.

This movie is pretty silly. It is a basically a collection of clips from horror, science fiction and suspense films. There are some addresses to the audience between the clips and Donald Pleasance and Nancy Travis are the audience. They try to be educational and explain the appeal of horror films. Not a bad idea but some the things they say ("horovies help us deal with real horror", "we are at the mercy of the people in the film") are pretty trite. Also the clips are shown very quickly and it can be kind of jarring. They are shown out of context, so they aren't very scary or interesting. And it's very short--I saw it at the Moody Theatre in Austin, Texas, and I can't believe I paid $2.50 for an 18 minute movie! Still, it is a fun movie, and Travis and Pleasance seem to be enjoying themselves. For people who have an interest in learning more about horror it might be fun and educational. But if you're a horror fan (like me) you'll probably be bored silly. Good idea, poor execution (no pun intended). I give it two stars.

Wow, what a cheesy movie this is! It starts off looking like it's gonna be a backwoods slasher, with the camera following dogs running through the woods. It then gets a bit boring and follows the story of some girls moving into some house haunted by Indian spirits. We then get plenty of shots of one partially clad girl and another naked girl in the bath. It suddenly gets really cheesy when the "Zombie Indians" arise from the earth and start terrorising the girls. We even get a samurai Indian. This movie starts off pretty boring although I did find the story of the four Indians who buried themselves alive quite interesting. Once the Indian zombies (or whatever you want to call them for they aren't technically zombies) start terrorising the girls is when all the fun begins. This is not a special flick and can't be taken seriously, it's just something fun to watch when you're bored or when you're drinking with friends. I can't help thinking though that it would have worked better as a short story because the first half is tediously boring.

Creakiness and atmosphere this film has, but so unfortunately does the print I just viewed. Raymond Massey provides a laid back Sherlock Holmes, almost comically so in early scenes in his bathrobe, which he trades in for a laborer's garb to investigate the creepy mansion of Dr. Rylott (Lyn Harding). What wasn't clear to me was why Rylott would have wanted his stepdaughters dead. If as in the case of Helen (Angela Baddeley), he didn't want her to run off to get married, he would have accomplished the same thing by having her dispatched. Other curiosities abound as well. After setting an early wedding date with Helen, the fiancée is no longer heard from for the rest of the picture. The presence of a band of gypsies at the time of Violet Stoner's death provides merely a diversion, and what could have been an interesting murder tool, a poisonous snake, is diluted by the fact that it was not a cobra, the musical renderings of the Indian man servant notwithstanding. Athole Stewart competently portrays Holmes' aide Dr. Watson, though he takes some getting used to if Nigel Bruce is more your cup of tea. As Rylott, Lyn Harding is sufficiently menacing, a trait that would be put to good use as Holmes' nemesis Professor Moriarty in two later films - 1935's "The Triumph of Sherlock Holmes" and 1937's "Murder at the Baskervilles". With repeated choppiness and an unsteady camera, it's surprising that the story line isn't more disrupted than it is. It's integrity is generally maintained, even if one stretches a bit to fill in the gaps. I guess that would be my main complaint with the film, as mentally bridging some of the jump cuts in the picture proved to be a real pain in the asp.

Steered text
The film's's atmosphere of mystery has held up so well in the print I just viewed. Raymond Massey provides a laid-back Sherlock Holmes, almostorably so in early scenes in his bathrobe, which he trades in for more traditional Holmes Holmes garb to confront the creepy figure of Dr. Rylott (Lyn Harding). It's not clear to me exactly why Rylott would have wanted his fiancee dead. If, as in the case of Helen (Angela Lansburyn), he didn't want her to meet Holmes and get married, he would have accomplished the same thing by having her killed. Other curiosities such as the mention of Holmes' early wedding date with Helen, though still present, are no longer a distraction for the rest of the film. The presence of a band of gypsies at the time of Miss Stoner's death provides for a diversion that leads to the resolution of the mystery. The mystery of the snake bite is resolved by the fact that it was not a cobra but the venomous snake that the doctor's servant kept. Athole Barnard well portrays Holmes' aide Dr. Watson, though he takes some getting used to if Nigel Bruce is not your cup of tea. As Rylott, Lyn Harding is sufficiently menacing, a quality that would be put to good use as Holmes' nemesis Professor Moriarty in two later films - 1935's "The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes" and 1937's "Hound at the Baskervilles." If Holmes were to stop and talk to the camera, it's unlikely that the story would be any more disrupted than it is. The narrative integrity is generally maintained, even if one does a bit to fill in the gaps. I suppose that would be my only criticism of the film, as though bridging some of the narrative gaps in the original novel would be a goal to which it aspires

Put simply, this mini-series was terrible. Let me count the ways. 1. Absurd plotting. 2. Over-acting. 3. Scattershot approach to characters. 4. Annoying narration. 5. Inability to create viewer interest. This film can't even pass the "Soap Opera for Dummies" test. I'm sorry I have not read this award-winning novel, so I am judging it only as a film, but it really stinks. Imagine going to a party where they show you dozens of appetizers. You look at the wide variety and want to taste them, but suddenly they are withdrawn, and you wonder where they went. That's like this film, with way too many characters introduced and never drawn out. There are enough stories and characters in this film to create a 20 episode series, yet we are given less than four hours to digest it all. There are more facial expressions and reaction shots of Ed Harris than you'll find on 10,000 monkeys. The pace is extraordinarily slow. Dennis Farina and Helen Hunt are so far over-the-top that their characters are not believable. Joanne Woodward's character is one-dimensional. The persistent river metaphor becomes trite. And, probably the most absurd part of the film--the cat. This evil and vengeful cat who follows the hero around to scratch him and his seat covers--well, come on now---it's not even good Stephen King! Probably the most interesting character in the film, and one who is not drawn well, is John Voss, the disturbed boy whose final act of desperation accounts for the only plot device that works in this film. Just about everyone in this film is unbelievable. To sum up, there's little here to inspire. The drama is poor melodrama. It's just a terrible effort.

My guess is that the producers of this low-budget space/horror film wanted a serious movie but the director had his heart set on a parody. So...this is what we get. Set in an abandoned spaceship 1000 years in the future and peopled with characters and props right out of the 90's. The set is some industrial complex, maybe an oil tanker, whatever. They use is AS IS so the controls consist racks of old TV equipment. One location is obviously the employees lunchroom and sports an old TV and VCR as well as a water cooler with plastic demijohn. Tiny Lister and Coolio get the best lines, arguing throughout the story. The dialog is packed with terms that are pretty dated even now ("A-OK, Daddy-O") but then maybe the 30th century is very retro? When the captain declares the ships cargo is a load of coffins from "The Transylvania Station" you know this is all a put-on. Its a bit of Alien, part JasonX, shameless rip-off of all the best sci-fi and horror titles. At one point Casper VanDien even tells his pilot to "make it so" with a straight face. This film would have been better if they had just let everyone run with the satire but they keep attempting to make the story serious....maybe the backers were on the set that day. Anyway, not a bad boredom killer if you aren't too picky. FX are as good as the sets are bad.

My guess is that the producers of this sci-fi space opera/comedy film wanted a serious movie but the director had his heart set on a comedy. So...this is what we get. The ship is abandoned for over 1000 years in the future and the crew is still alive and trying to figure out the out of the ship. The set is an industrial complex, maybe an oil tanker or whatever. The use is AS IS so the controls consist racks of old TV sets. One location is like the employees lunchroom and has an old TV and VCR as well as a coffee machine and a demijohn. Dave Lister and Coolio get the best lines, arguing throughout the story. The movie is packed with jokes that are pretty dated by now ("A-OK, Daddy-O") but thats maybe the point. The social satire is pretty good. When the captain says the ships cargo is a load of coffins from "The Wizard of Oz" you know this is not a put-on. Its a bit campy, a bit cheesy, but it has some of the years best sci-fi and comedy moments. At one point Casper VanDien even tells his crew to "make it so" with a straight face. Though a fan of shock and gore, I found this movie disappointing to say the very least. The effects and puppet work were impressive, yes, and the humor was well-timed, but... something was missing. See, the first act of the film is spent establishing nuances of Jack Brooks' character, despite the fact that everything we need to know about his aggression is delivered within minutes of the first title cards. As for the narration and many of the flashbacks: needless. The pacing during the second act was tedious. Most of it is focused on Freddy Krueger eating, then vomiting, then eating some more, then flailing his arms and saying something snappy or rude. All the while, the schlock is punctuated with brief scenes of Jack discussing his rage problems with a therapist. (Definitely the entertaining scenes in the film -- excellent dialog worth plenty of laughs.) Then, without warning, Jack decides to kill a few monsters. And then it's over. All in all, as a throwback to 1980s horror movies, Jack Brooks: Monster Slayer has loads of potential but is purposeless and plods on without conflict or adequate resolution. Hopefully, these issues will be addressed before Jack Brooks VII: Jack Goes to Hell or Jack vs. Ash go into production.

Though I do enjoy horror and gore, I found this movie to be very, very disappointing. The effects and camera work were impressive, sure, and the humor was well-timed, but... something was missing. The first act of the movie focuses on establishing nuances of Jack Brooks' character, despite the fact none of it matters. All of his aggression is delivered succinctly in the first few cards. As for his friends and many of the monsters, they disappear. The pacing during the second act was terrible. Most of the movie focused on Freddy the Clown eating, then vomiting, then eating some more, then cutting off his arms and legs for being lazy or rude. All the while, the movie is interspersed with brief scenes of Jack discussing his rage problems with his friends. (Definitely most entertaining scenes in the movie -- excellent dialog worth plenty of laughs.) Then, without warning, Jack decides to kill a few monsters. And then it's over. All in all, as a throwback to the classic 80s monster movies, Jack Brooks: Monster Slayer has loads of potential, but the movie just plods along without conflict or real resolution. Hopefully, these issues are addressed when future Jack Brooks movies like Jack Goes to Hell or Jack vs. Frankenstein go into production

It may, however, help to explain the way in which many American spectators behaved at the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics and the TV coverage which seemed only interested in events that Americans were likely to win.

I caught this on IFC last week and I thought it was typical of the indie short subject film: heavy on style, little on substance and originality. Plus, this film wallows in late 1970s chic, which works for some (Sofia Coppola's "The Virgin Suicides" comes to mind) but not for this director. Another reviewer compared this to Harmony Korine's work and I agree. Yet I don't view this as a positive thing (what has HE done lately, anyway?). "Bobbycrush" is really just a waste of time and energy for all involved. If you happen to see it late night on cable, turn the channel and watch something else instead.

I was in Blockbuster and I saw a film called "Dark Harvest". The cover art looked great, the plot wasn't that bad, and the tagline (You reap what you sow) made the movie look pretty good. But I was dumb that day, because I did something I should have never done. I rented a "Straight To Video Independent Horror Film" Walking out with my much better rentals, I went home, popped Dark Harvest in the DVD player and it began. I figured I would watch the trailer after the film was done (BAD IDEA) but went ahead and watched it anyway. NOW to the review.*POSSIBLE SPOILERS* First off, the acting by the "kids" sucks, and the scene when the 2 (main characters) are talking, the lighting sucks, and the buildings even look fake! Now they go to this house, where Sean Connel's (I think he's the main character, I don't care) relatives lived there. All of a sudden one by one, they all start getting killed by...(gasp) A KILLER SCARECROW!!!! AHHH!!!!! The scarecrow is obviously the definition of low budget, and the scenes where the scarecrow is computerized looks so fake it's hilarious. It makes dinosaur noises and everything! And then at the end...they shoot the scarecrow with a gun (that is red for god's sake and looks like it was purchased at a local family dollar) and it pauses for a while and then.....(gasp) BLOWS UP!!!!!! Save yourself some time, I'm telling you this movie sucks. if you need to pass an hour and a half, look at the wall, because looking at the wall is A+ fun compared to this disaster. It is quite funny though. Overall Grade: F If there was anything lower **F-** Than I would give it that.

I was at the theater and I saw a movie called "Dark Harvest". The box cover looked great, the plot wasn't too bad, and the tagline (You reap what you sow) made the movie sound pretty good. But I must say that the only thing I did not do was watch this movie. I rented a "Straight to Video, Independent Film" Walking Dead for my much better experience. I went to the theater, put in the movie, and it started. I figured I would watch it, and when it was done (BAD IDEA) I went home and watched it again. NOW to the movie.*POSSIBLE SPOILERS* First, I was shocked by the "kids" acting, and the scene when the 2 (gasp) kids die, the acting sucks, and the buildings even look fake! Now we get to the house, where Sean Connel's (I think that's the main character, I'm not sure) family are there and all of a sudden one by one, they are all getting killed by (gasp) A COMPUTERIZED SCARECROW!!!! AHHH!!!! The worst part is that the movie looks low budget, and the scenes where the scarecrow is computerized looks so fake it's hilarious. It has moving eyes and everything, and then at the end when they shoot a gun at the scarecrow (which is red for some reason, and looks like it was made at a 5 dollar store) it pauses for a second and then.....(gasp) BLOWS UP!!!!!! Please, save yourself some time. I'm telling you this movie is great if you want to pass an hour and a half, and have a laugh, because "Dark Harvest" is A+ fun for a bad movie. It's not funny though. Overall Rating: If I could give it **0** stars, I would give it.

That is why this anime fails!

This movie is based on the game Street Fighter Alpha (or something)! It takes place in an other setting than that of the animated movie. This movie is all about Ryu who is a martial artist and his friends. I recognized most of the characters in this movie! They are the majority of the characters from the video game (that I could recognize). The fighting scenes in this movie were really spectacular! And there were so many of them! For me this is the main thing that I like about this movie. The original animated movie (1994) is also referenced in this movie. The fighting scenes are more realistic in this movie! The use of the "Street ofken" and other supernatural powers are used. characters are shown with skills that they have in the video game! All in all this movie is a great movie! But there is one thing that I don't really like about this movie. The violence is toned down considerably! Why? And what happened to the other characters from the video game? Surely there is more than just Ryu in the story? The main attraction of the video game are the characters with their unique fighting skills! In this movie it's all about Ryu! Also, why the anime?
